title: Lab 229 - Linux Logical Volume Management - LVM

lab_objective.description: By completing this lab, you will learn how to:
objectives: Identify a newly attached disk using lsblk
Create a GPT partition table using gdisk
Create four GPT partitions on a disk
Set Linux LVM GPT partition types
Create and manage a Volume Group (VG)
Create and manage a Logical Volume (LV)
Create an XFS filesystem on an LVM logical volume
Extend a logical volume using free space already available in a Volume Group
Extend an XFS filesystem after increasing the logical volume
Add an additional partition as an LVM Physical Volume
Extend an existing Volume Group with an additional Physical Volume
Extend a logical volume using newly added Volume Group capacity
Verify LVM configuration using pvs, vgs, lvs, lsblk, df, and findmnt
scenario: You are working as a Linux Systems Administrator responsible for preparing additional storage for an application server.
A new 2 GB disk has been attached to the server as /dev/sdb.
The application requires a dedicated filesystem mounted at /data.
The storage team has requested that the disk be managed using Linux Logical Volume Management (LVM) so that the filesystem can be expanded in the future without rebuilding the filesystem.
The disk must initially be divided into four GPT partitions.
/dev/sdb1, /dev/sdb2, and /dev/sdb3 will initially be configured as LVM Physical Volumes and added to the volume group vg_db.
/dev/sdb4 will initially remain unused and reserved for future storage expansion.
A logical volume named lv_db will be created inside vg_db and formatted with XFS.
The filesystem will be mounted at /data and configured to remain available after a system reboot.
Later in the lab, /dev/sdb4 will be initialized as an LVM Physical Volume, added to vg_db, and used to provide additional capacity to lv_db.

tasks.title: Identify the New Disk
steps: Use an appropriate command to display the available disks and their sizes.
Identify the newly attached 2 GB disk that will be used for this lab.
The disk must be /dev/sdb.
Do not modify /dev/sda or any disk containing the operating system.
Verify the total size of /dev/sdb before continuing.

tasks.title: Create a GPT Partition Table and Four Partitions
steps: Start gdisk on /dev/sdb.
Use gdisk help (?) when needed.
Create a new GPT partition table on /dev/sdb.
Create four GPT partitions: /dev/sdb1, /dev/sdb2, /dev/sdb3, and /dev/sdb4.
The first three partitions should each be approximately 512 MB.
Create /dev/sdb4 using the remaining available disk space.
All four partitions must collectively use the available space on /dev/sdb.
Set the GPT partition type of all four partitions to Linux LVM.
Use GPT partition type code 8E00 for Linux LVM.
Verify the partition table before writing the changes.
Write the partition table to /dev/sdb and exit gdisk.
Run partprobe so that the kernel detects the new partition table without rebooting.

tasks.title: Create the Initial Physical Volumes
steps: Create an LVM Physical Volume on /dev/sdb1.
Create an LVM Physical Volume on /dev/sdb2.
Create an LVM Physical Volume on /dev/sdb3.
Do not initialize /dev/sdb4 as an LVM Physical Volume at this stage.
Use pvs to verify the Physical Volumes.
Verify that /dev/sdb1, /dev/sdb2, and /dev/sdb3 appear as LVM Physical Volumes.
Verify that /dev/sdb4 does not yet appear as an LVM Physical Volume.

tasks.title: Create the Volume Group
steps: Create a Volume Group named vg_db.
Use /dev/sdb1, /dev/sdb2, and /dev/sdb3 as the Physical Volumes for vg_db.
Display the Volume Group information.
Use vgs and/or vgdisplay to verify the configuration.
Verify that vg_db exists.
Verify that vg_db contains exactly three Physical Volumes.
Verify that vg_db has available free space for creating and extending Logical Volumes.

tasks.title: Create the Logical Volume
steps: Create a Logical Volume named lv_db inside vg_db.
Allocate approximately 1 GB of the currently available free space to lv_db from the vg_db volume group.
Do not consume all available space in vg_db.
Verify that /dev/vg_db/lv_db exists.
Use lvs to display the Logical Volume information.
Verify that lv_db belongs to vg_db.
Verify that the Volume Group retains free space after creating lv_db.

tasks.title: Create the XFS Filesystem and Mount /data
steps: Create an XFS filesystem on /dev/vg_db/lv_db.
Verify that the Logical Volume contains an XFS filesystem.
Create the /data directory as the mount point.
Verify that /data exists and is a directory.
Mount /dev/vg_db/lv_db on /data.
Verify that the filesystem is mounted successfully.
Use df -hT to verify the filesystem type, capacity, and mount point.
Redirect the df -hT output to /home/your_username/lv_db_mount.
Verify that the redirected output file was created successfully.

tasks.title: Configure Persistent Mounting Using /etc/fstab
steps: Configure /etc/fstab so that /dev/vg_db/lv_db is automatically mounted on /data after a reboot.
Use /dev/vg_db/lv_db as the device specification in /etc/fstab.
Use XFS as the filesystem type.
Use the defaults mount option.
Configure the entry so that no dump is performed.
Configure the entry so that no filesystem check is performed at boot.
Verify the /etc/fstab entry before rebooting.
Test the /etc/fstab configuration without rebooting the system.
Verify that /data mounts successfully without errors.

tasks.title: Extend lv_db Using Free Space in vg_db
steps: Before extending lv_db, check its current size.
Verify that vg_db has sufficient free space.
Extend /dev/vg_db/lv_db by 500 MB and use -r option to resize the XFS filesystem so that it uses the additional Logical Volume capacity.
Do not initialize or add /dev/sdb4 at this stage.
Verify that the Logical Volume size increased.
Verify the updated filesystem size.
Verify the filesystem type and mount point.
Use df -hT to verify the increased capacity and redirect the output to /home/your_username/lv_db_extend.
Verify that the redirected output file was created successfully.

tasks.title: Initialize /dev/sdb4 as an LVM Physical Volume
steps: The fourth partition, /dev/sdb4, was intentionally left unused during the initial LVM configuration.
The storage team has now provided /dev/sdb4 for additional application capacity.
Create an LVM Physical Volume on /dev/sdb4.
Use pvs to verify that /dev/sdb4 appears as an LVM Physical Volume.
Verify that /dev/sdb1, /dev/sdb2, /dev/sdb3, and /dev/sdb4 are now recognized as LVM Physical Volumes.
Do not create another Volume Group.

tasks.title: Add /dev/sdb4 to vg_db
steps: Extend the existing vg_db Volume Group by adding /dev/sdb4.
Do not create a second Volume Group.
Use vgs and/or vgdisplay to verify the Volume Group.
Verify that vg_db now contains four Physical Volumes.
Verify that /dev/sdb4 belongs to vg_db.
Verify that the total size of vg_db increased after adding /dev/sdb4.
Verify the updated Physical Volume, Volume Group, and free-space information.

tasks.title: Extend lv_db Using the Newly Added Capacity
steps: Extend /dev/vg_db/lv_db using 100% of the available free space in vg_db.
Do not create a second Logical Volume.
Do not use the -r option when extending the Logical Volume.
Verify that lv_db increased in size.
Extend the existing XFS filesystem so that it uses the newly allocated Logical Volume capacity.
The existing filesystem must remain XFS.
The existing filesystem must remain mounted at /data.
Verify that the XFS filesystem size increased.
Verify that the filesystem size reflects the latest Logical Volume size.
Use lvs to verify the final Logical Volume size.
Use vgs to verify that the available free space in vg_db has been consumed appropriately.
Use df -hT to verify the final filesystem size, filesystem type, and /data mount point.

completion_message: Great job! Lab 229 completed successfully. You practiced the complete LVM workflow, including GPT partitioning, Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, Logical Volumes, XFS filesystems, persistent mounting, extending Logical Volumes using existing VG space, adding a new Physical Volume, extending the Volume Group, and expanding the filesystem.
